details:
**October Crisis**
In 1970 the Quebec separatist group FLQ (Front de libération du Québec) kidnapped British diplomat James Cross and Quebec Deputy Premier Pierre Laporte, whom they killed. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act, and when asked how far he would go he replied "Just watch me."

**Pacific Scandal**
The 1873 scandal in which Canada's first prime minister, John A. Macdonald, was revealed to have taken election money from railway tycoon Hugh Allan, who sought the contract to build the transcontinental railway. A stolen telegram exposed the deal, Macdonald resigned, and the Liberals took power for the first time.

**Louis Riel and the Métis rebellions**
Riel led the Métis, a people of mixed Indigenous and European descent, in the 1869–1870 Red River Rebellion, during which his provisional government executed the Ontario loyalist Thomas Scott; the Wolseley expedition was sent to restore order. He returned to lead the 1885 North-West Rebellion with Gabriel Dumont, who won at Duck Lake, and was hanged under Macdonald's government.

**Conscription Crises**
Robert Borden's introduction of conscription in 1917 during World War I bitterly divided English and French Canada, leading to the 1918 Easter riots in Quebec City; Henri Bourassa was a leading French-Canadian opponent. William Lyon Mackenzie King faced a second Conscription Crisis in 1944.

**Battle of the Plains of Abraham**
The 1759 battle outside Quebec City in which British general James Wolfe defeated the French under the Marquis de Montcalm; both commanders were killed. It led to the British conquest of New France.

**New France and the King's Daughters**
The French colony along the St. Lawrence, whose capital Quebec City was founded by Samuel de Champlain in 1608. Intendant Jean Talon helped bring about 800 young women, the King's Daughters (Filles du Roi), to boost the population; the colony also featured the seigneurial land system and fur-trading coureurs des bois.

**Quebec sovereignty and the Quiet Revolution**
Quebec underwent rapid secularization and modernization in the 1960s Quiet Revolution under Premier Jean Lesage, following the conservative "Great Darkness" of Maurice Duplessis. Separatism grew, Charles de Gaulle proclaimed "Vive le Québec libre!" at Expo 67, and independence referendums failed in 1980 and narrowly in 1995 under Prime Minister Jean Chrétien.

**William Lyon Mackenzie King**
Canada's longest-serving prime minister, who led the country through World War II and secretly sought advice from spirits, including those of his dead dogs, all named Pat. In the 1926 King–Byng affair, Governor General Julian Byng refused his request to dissolve Parliament and invited Arthur Meighen to form a government, causing a constitutional crisis.

**Juno Beach and the Dieppe Raid**
In World War II, Canadian troops, including the Queen's Own Rifles, landed at Juno Beach on D-Day in 1944; most of the ground forces in the disastrous 1942 Dieppe Raid were also Canadian. The Netherlands sent Canada tulips after the war in thanks for liberating the country and sheltering its royal family.

**If Day**
A staged mock Nazi invasion and occupation of Winnipeg in February 1942, organized to promote the sale of Victory Bonds for Canada's war effort.

**Battle of Vimy Ridge**
An April 1917 World War I battle in France in which all four divisions of the Canadian Corps fought together for the first time and captured the ridge, an event often seen as a birth of Canadian national identity.

**Halifax Explosion**
On December 6, 1917, the French munitions ship SS Mont-Blanc collided with another vessel in the harbor of Halifax, Nova Scotia, and exploded, killing about 2,000 people in one of the largest man-made explosions before the atomic bomb.

**Rebellions of 1837 and the Family Compact**
William Lyon Mackenzie led a rebellion in Upper Canada (now Ontario) against the Family Compact, a conservative elite associated with John Robinson; during it the American steamship Caroline, supplying the rebels, was set ablaze. The rebellions led to reforms that paved the way for Confederation in 1867.

**Fenian Raids and United Empire Loyalists**
United Empire Loyalists who backed Britain fled to Canada after the American Revolution, settling largely in Upper Canada. Canada was later targeted by the Fenian Raids (1866–1871), invasions by Irish-American nationalists hoping to pressure Britain over Irish independence.

**Lester Pearson and Brian Mulroney**
Lester Pearson won the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize for resolving the Suez Crisis with a UN peacekeeping force, later became prime minister, and saw his proposed flag mocked as the "Pearson Pennant." Brian Mulroney won the 1984 election after telling John Turner "You had an option, sir" over patronage appointments, and his term was marred by the failure of the Meech Lake Accord on Quebec's constitutional status.
